A skiff is a small, simple, open boat — the kind a single person can easily handle on their own. Think of it as the most basic, no-frills boat you can imagine: no cabin, no roof, no fancy equipment. Just a lightweight vessel that gets you across the water.

A skiff typically has a flat or nearly flat bottom, which means it sits very shallow in the water rather than cutting deep into it like a sailboat or a ship. Because of this, it doesn't need much water beneath it to float — a few inches to a foot is often enough. This makes it perfect for rivers, lakes, ponds, marshes, and calm coastal areas where the water is too shallow for bigger boats.

It is usually narrow, open from end to end (you can see straight in — there's no covered deck), and light enough that one person can drag it up onto a shore or beach without much effort.

A skiff can be:

  • Rowed with oars (the classic way)
  • Powered by a small outboard motor attached to the back
  • Sailed with a small sail, in some designs
  • Poled — pushed along with a long pole in very shallow water

There's no single "correct" method. The skiff is versatile and straightforward.

The skiff is essentially a working person's boat. Its most common uses are:

  • Fishing — especially in shallow rivers, bays, and lakes. A fisherman can row out quietly, cast a line, and move around easily.
  • Short crossings — getting from one bank of a river to the other, or reaching a small island nearby.
  • As a companion to a larger vessel — bigger ships often carry a small skiff on board (sometimes called a tender) to let sailors row ashore when the ship can't dock directly.
  • General errands on water — in coastal and riverside communities, the skiff was historically the equivalent of a small car: an everyday, practical tool for getting things done.

If you've ever sat in a small rowboat on a lake — a simple, wooden or aluminum boat with two oars and room for two or three people at most — you've essentially been in something very close to a skiff. It's intimate with the water. Because it sits so low and shallow, you can almost touch the surface with your hand over the side. It moves quietly. It's not built for the open ocean or rough seas — it's built for calm, sheltered water where you need something light, simple, and reliable.

A large ocean liner is to a skiff what a truck is to a bicycle.

In Ernest Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, the old fisherman Santiago goes out alone into the Gulf Stream in a skiff — a small, simple boat he rows by himself. The word captures his solitude and the modest, humble nature of his life perfectly. That image — one old man, one small boat, the vast ocean — is a good one to hold onto when you think of the word.

In some regional British dialects (particularly in northern England and Scotland), skiff can also refer to a light, brief shower — a very slight fall of rain or snow that barely amounts to anything. "There was just a skiff of snow overnight." This usage is relatively rare and regional, so if you encounter the word without a nautical context, this might be what's meant — but in most cases, across most of the English-speaking world, skiff = small boat.

• "He tied the skiff to the dock and walked up to the house."
  • "They crossed the river in a small skiff, taking turns at the oars."
  • "The fisherman's skiff was barely big enough for two men and their gear."

In short: A skiff is a small, flat-bottomed, open boat — light, simple, and suited for calm, shallow water. It's the most elemental form of a boat: just you, a vessel, and the water.
